content: Leukopenia, also referred to as a deficiency in white blood cells (WBCs), leukocytes, or low WBC count, encompasses a reduction in the absolute number of leukocytes in the blood. This condition may involve granulocytes (such as neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils) or lymphocytes (including T-cells and B-cells). In most cases, leukopenia is primarily due to neutropenia, as neutrophils constitute the majority of leukocytes. Since the primary role of white blood cells is to combat infections, a decrease in their number significantly increases a patient’s susceptibility to infections. In pancytopenia, other blood cell types, such as red blood cells and platelets, are also affected alongside white blood cells. Neutropenia specifically refers to a reduction in circulating neutrophil granulocytes, which are the most abundant type of white blood cells. While the terms leukopenia and neutropenia are sometimes used interchangeably, neutropenia is more accurately considered a subset of leukopenia. This distinction is important because the neutrophil count is the most critical indicator of infection risk. Low white blood cell counts are commonly associated with chemotherapy, radiation therapy, leukemia (where malignant cells overwhelm the bone marrow), myelofibrosis, and aplastic anemia (conditions characterized by the failure of white and red blood cell production, as well as poor platelet production). Additionally, many commonly used medications can induce leukopenia. Other causes of low white blood cell counts include viral infections such as influenza, HIV, and dengue; bacterial infections like tuberculosis and typhus; systemic lupus erythematosus; Rickettsial infections; splenomegaly (enlargement of the spleen); folate deficiencies; and sepsis. Numerous other etiologies also exist. Leukopenia is typically diagnosed through a complete blood count (CBC), which provides a detailed analysis of the various blood cell types.
